prompt: In cache-aside, who loads data into the cache on a miss?

options.text: The application code, after reading the database
The cache itself, using a registered loader function
The database, by pushing rows through a trigger
Nobody; cache-aside only caches values on writes

explanation: In cache-aside the cache is passive; the application reads the database on a miss and stores the result. (b) describes read-through. (c) Databases don't push into the cache in this pattern. (d) Cache-aside is primarily a read pattern; writes just invalidate.

scenario: A service uses cache-aside with Redis. The Redis cluster becomes unreachable for ten minutes. The code treats any cache error as a miss.

options.text: All reads fail with errors until Redis comes back, since every read goes through it
Reads still succeed from the database, just slower, and it takes the full read load
Reads return slightly stale data from Redis's on-disk snapshot until it recovers
Writes fail because the cache delete errors, but reads carry on exactly as before

explanation: Cache-aside falls back to the source of truth, so reads stay correct; the real danger is whether the database can absorb 100% of reads. (a) would only happen if cache errors weren't handled; here they are treated as misses. (c) Unreachable means nothing is served from Redis at all, snapshot or not. (d) Writes go to the database and only the delete fails, while reads are definitely affected in latency and load.

prompt: What is a practical advantage of a read-through cache library over hand-written cache-aside?

options.text: It lets the cache act as the source of truth, so the database is consulted far less often
Loading logic lives in one place, and concurrent misses for a key coalesce into one load
It guarantees the cache is never stale, because the library loads every value itself
It makes writes faster, because the library batches them on the way to the database

explanation: Read-through centralises the miss path and good libraries coalesce concurrent loads. (a) The database is still the source of truth; the cache only holds copies. (c) Staleness still depends on invalidation and TTLs; loading on a miss says nothing about later updates. (d) Read-through is about reads; write speed depends on the write strategy.

prompt: Under write-through, when is the client told the write succeeded?

options.text: As soon as the cache has the value, before the database
After both the cache and the database have the value
After the next read of the key confirms the new value
After the database has it, before the cache is updated

explanation: Write-through is synchronous to both stores. (a) describes write-behind. (c) No standard write strategy waits for a later read. (d) Acknowledging before the cache is written is closer to write-around; write-through waits for both.

prompt: Which statements about write-through are true? (Choose all that apply.)

options.text: A read straight after a write is usually a hit with the new value
Each write pays the latency of both the cache and the database
It guarantees cache and database can never disagree
It can fill the cache with values nobody reads, so a TTL is still useful

explanation: (a) The written value is placed in the cache. (b) Both hops are synchronous. (d) Every write is cached, read or not. (c) is false: the two updates aren't atomic, so a crash between them or concurrent writers in different orders can leave them out of step.

prompt: How many acknowledged writes could be lost?
scenario: A write-behind cache takes 8,000 writes a second, spread evenly across 4 nodes, and flushes each node's dirty entries to the database every 3 seconds. One node crashes just before its flush.

options.text: About 2,000
About 6,000
About 24,000
None, because the writes were acknowledged

explanation: The node receives 8,000 ÷ 4 = 2,000 writes a second, and up to 3 seconds are unflushed: 6,000. (a) counts only one second. (c) counts all four nodes. (d) is the trap: under write-behind, acknowledged means 'in the cache', not 'durable'.

prompt: Which data is the safest fit for write-behind?
scenario: A social app is considering write-behind for four kinds of writes: new user sign-ups, payment captures, per-post view counters, and direct messages.

options.text: New user sign-up records
Payment capture records
Per-post view counters
Direct messages between users

explanation: View counters are high-rate, benefit from batching, and losing a few seconds of increments is harmless. (a) A lost sign-up means a user who was told their account exists has none. (b) Losing a captured payment is a financial error. (d) Users notice and care about lost messages.

prompt: Which write strategy fits this data best?
scenario: An audit service writes 30,000 audit events a second. Fewer than 1% are ever read, usually weeks later during an investigation. The service also caches hot user records in the same Redis cluster.

options.text: Write-through, so every event is in the cache for fast lookups later
Write-behind, so the 30,000 writes a second are batched to the database
Write-around: write events only to the database; rare reads fill the cache
Cache every event with no TTL so investigations never touch the database

explanation: Write-around keeps rarely read data out of the cache, so it doesn't evict the hot user records. (a) would flood the cache with 30,000 entries a second that are almost never read. (b) still fills the cache and risks losing acknowledged audit events, which defeats their purpose. (d) is (a) made worse: the cache fills and evicts everything useful.

prompt: Why is 'update the database, then delete the cache key' called write-around?

options.text: The write goes around the cache to the database, and the cache refills only on a later read
The write goes to the cache only and goes around the database until a later flush
Writes travel clockwise around a ring of cache nodes until the node that owns the key stores them
The cache writes around to the database on a timer, batching dirty keys together

explanation: The cache isn't written; the database is, and a later miss reloads. (b) describes write-behind, where the database is skipped until a flush. (c) confuses this with consistent hashing. (d) describes write-behind flushing.

prompt: Which design is the best starting point?
scenario: You're adding a cache for product pages: 50,000 reads a second, about 20 product edits a minute, edits by staff who don't mind a few seconds' delay, and a database that can handle about 10,000 reads a second.

options.text: Cache-aside reads, update the database then delete the key on edits, plus a TTL
Write-behind for product edits, so staff edits return instantly from the cache
No cache; let the database serve all 50,000 reads and add indexes for speed
Write-through with no TTL, so every edit lands in the cache immediately

explanation: A hugely read-heavy workload with rare edits that tolerate slight delay is the textbook case for cache-aside with delete on write and a TTL safety net. (b) risks losing edits to save time nobody needs saved. (c) The database can handle about 10,000 reads a second, five times too few, and indexes don't change that. (d) Write-through without a TTL lets any missed update or race persist forever.

prompt: Which strategy carries a durability risk from the cache itself?

options.text: Cache-aside
Write-through
Write-around
Write-behind

explanation: Only write-behind acknowledges writes before the database has them. (a) and (c) write the database directly. (b) writes the database synchronously before acknowledging.
